\NLFrontMatterSection{Executive summary}

This register documents a primary failure condition, potential consequence, mitigation strategy, assurance evidence, accountable owner, and preliminary attention band for every unique controlled requirement and component in the NL-TPS suite. Functional/non-functional/operational requirement IDs are retained as aliases to their 119 source HLRs and 357 source detailed requirements, avoiding duplicate risk records while preserving trace.

The register covers 119 system HLRs, 357 detailed sub-requirements, 357 high-level interface requirements, 1,071 sub-interface requirements, 45 functional components, 61 interface components, and 78 category-scoped components. The source requirement or component responsibility remains normative; this register describes the risk of failure and the minimum control intent associated with it.

\begin{nlnotice}{PRELIMINARY RISK STATUS}
Attention bands prioritize multidisciplinary review; they are not risk acceptability classifications. The 119 HLR score records remain pending approved multidisciplinary facilitated analysis. Child scores inherit only from an approved HLR score, with a controlled override and exception record; component scores use the maximum approved linked HLR score. Gate 1 and later remain blocked until all 119 parent scores and acceptance decisions are approved.
\end{nlnotice}

\section{Purpose, scope, and interpretation}

The register supports process mapping, hazard analysis, FMEA, fault trees, architecture decisions, interface controls, verification planning, commissioning, cybersecurity, human-factors engineering, monitoring, incident response, change control, and release review. A row does not replace the full source obligation, linked hazards, or required evidence.

Risk is evaluated for the reasonably foreseeable failure of the requirement or component responsibility. Mitigation follows a control hierarchy: inherent safety and authority boundaries; deterministic prevention and fail-closed behavior; protected state and data integrity; detection, warning, quarantine, and reconciliation; professional review and independent QA; recovery; and governed information, training, and procedures.

\section{Risk-control completion and residual-risk rule}

A mitigation is not effective merely because it is specified or implemented. Effectiveness requires traceable verification under representative and failure conditions, site commissioning where applicable, monitoring with controlled thresholds, anomaly disposition, and confirmation that the control does not introduce unacceptable new risk. Control independence, common-cause failure, automation bias, alert burden, cybersecurity, downtime, and recovery shall be included in the evaluation.

No clinical release may rely on an unapproved numerical risk score, an automatically generated risk acceptance, or a trade-off score as a substitute for professional judgment and governance. Residual risk and benefit-risk decisions shall identify the approved criteria, evidence, uncertainty, affected population and scope, decision authority, limitations, monitoring, and revalidation triggers.
